text: Add regression-versus-previous-milestone and publish-only target kinds to the benchmark register so milestone gates can express 'no regression greater than N%' without restating numbers.
Decide the license for the benchmark dataset and hardware compatibility database (CC0 or ODbL).
rationale: Both are published community datasets and need reuse terms.

lens: Build, toolchain, CI and test infrastructure
text: Stand up a dedicated performance CI fleet of quiet bare-metal machines with fixed CPU frequency, disabled turbo and SMT policies documented, isolated from other CI load.
rationale: Microsecond-scale IPC and component-creation targets cannot be measured on shared or virtualised runners.

lens: Build, toolchain, CI and test infrastructure
text: Store all benchmark results in a time-series database with change-point detection, noise-calibrated thresholds and automatic bisection to the offending commit.
rationale: §54 demands every claim have a benchmark and a benchmark that nobody watches cannot catch regressions.

lens: Build, toolchain, CI and test infrastructure
text: Define a blocking performance gate: a regression beyond the calibrated noise band on tier-one benchmarks (IPC round trip, component creation, app startup, input-to-photon) blocks merge unless an ADR-linked exception is recorded.
rationale: Performance is a stated architectural claim and must be protected with the same rigour as correctness.

lens: Build, toolchain, CI and test infrastructure
text: Track kernel image size, initial image size and boot time to first frame as budgeted metrics with regression alerts.
rationale: Cheap isolation and fast startup claims degrade invisibly through bloat unless size and boot time are watched.

lens: Boot, firmware, platform security and identity
text: Set and track a disk-encryption overhead target (e.g. under 10% sequential and random NVMe throughput loss with AES-NI) in the benchmark suite.
rationale: Encryption by default is only defensible if its performance cost is measured and bounded.

lens: Boot, firmware, platform security and identity
text: Set and track boot-to-login and unlock-to-usable-desktop latency targets (for example under 10 s from firmware handoff to greeter on reference hardware, under 500 ms from unlock to interactive desktop) in the benchmark suite.
rationale: Verity, measured boot and encryption each add boot cost, and §54 demands that every architectural claim carry a benchmark.

text: Desktop-essentials latency targets tracked in the benchmark suite: keystroke-to-glyph through the IME path, notification post-to-display, lock-to-unlock, Wi-Fi reconnect after resume, Bluetooth audio connect, and camera cold start.
rationale: §54 tracks kernel and compositor metrics but the metrics users actually feel are these desktop-service latencies.

text: Run a public benchmark dashboard fed by CI with per-commit history and regression alerting for every metric in the performance requirements.
rationale: Performance claims must be continuously measured and publicly visible to be believed.

text: Set and measure an installation target: full install to first login in under 10 minutes on reference hardware from USB 3 media, tracked in the benchmark suite.
rationale: Installation time is the first performance impression a user forms and is trivially comparable to Windows and mainstream distros.

text: Benchmark interoperability paths against Linux and Windows on the same hardware: NTFS and exFAT throughput, SMB client throughput, VM guest application launch time and GPU fraction, and migration import time per 100 GB with verification.
rationale: §54 requires benchmarks for architectural claims and the compatibility layers are where users most expect regressions.

lens: Research spikes and decisions that must precede commitments
text: Set a numeric IPC round-trip target (e.g. same-core small-message round-trip under 1 µs, cross-core under 5 µs) as a V0 exit criterion.
rationale: The baseline names component creation and startup targets but leaves IPC, its highest-priority performance subsystem, without a number to hold the design to.

lens: Research spikes and decisions that must precede commitments
text: Build a physical input-to-photon measurement rig (photodiode plus microcontroller) and a pinned benchmark hardware set so latency claims are reproducible across releases.
rationale: Compositor and UI latency targets are meaningless without a measurement method independent of software timestamps.

lens: Research spikes and decisions that must precede commitments
text: Define the energy measurement methodology (external power meter, battery drain workloads, comparison OS images on the same laptop) before energy is tracked as a metric.
rationale: Energy is a listed tracked metric but is uniquely easy to mismeasure and must be defined before laptop targets are set.

text: Do not frame the project as 'rewrite Linux faster'; performance claims must come from semantic change, not reimplementation.
Component creation must be extremely cheap: target tens to hundreds of microseconds, measured and tracked per build.
Benchmark: component creation latency and memory overhead with comparison against Linux fork/exec, clone and container start.
Benchmark small-message IPC round-trip latency (same core and cross core) against Linux pipes, Unix sockets, io_uring and Fuchsia/seL4 published numbers.
Benchmark large-payload MemoryObject transfer cost versus memcpy and versus Linux shared memory + fd passing.
Demonstrate the same underlying physical memory used from NIC to GPU where hardware permits, and measure copies per stage.
Benchmark the V0 demo pipeline (Component A → Channel<Request> → Component B → MemoryObject transfer → result) for copies, latency and memory overhead.
Measure submit-to-completion latency for a no-op Operation and for Timer/Wait Operations, and track it as a standing benchmark.
Demonstrate 500,000 concurrent Tasks in one Component without 500,000 kernel threads, and measure memory per Task and creation latency.
Measure Task creation latency and Task switch latency and track them as standing benchmarks against Tokio tasks, Go goroutines, and Linux threads (cross-ref §54).
Measure wakeup-to-run scheduling latency per intent class under load and track it as a standing benchmark.
Measure ResourceDomain creation and teardown latency and track it as a standing benchmark (a component of isolation cost in §53).
Tracing must impose extremely low overhead; measure the cost of disabled tracepoints and of enabled tracing on IPC round-trip and Task switch, and set a budget.
Benchmark candidate filesystems for snapshot creation time, clone time, checksum overhead, and dedup effectiveness on a representative system image.
Measure generation creation time and disk overhead per generation and track them as standing benchmarks.
Measure service restart-to-rebind latency for the compositor and audio server and track as standing benchmarks.
Click-to-visible-UI must feel effectively immediate for native applications; define and measure the metric from launch request to first presented frame.
A simple native application must achieve warm startup under 20 ms (launch request to first presented frame), tracked as a standing benchmark.

Build a startup benchmark harness measuring warm and cold launch for the reference native apps (Terminal, Editor, Image Viewer) against equivalent Linux, Windows, and macOS applications (cross-ref §54).
Define the measurement boundary for 'visible UI' (first compositor presentation of a non-blank frame) so startup numbers are comparable across apps and systems.
Measure cold startup (content not in page cache) for simple native applications and set a target separately from the warm target.
Profile the launch path breakdown (Component creation, capability attachment, mapping, runtime init, first frame) to identify where the 20 ms budget is spent.
Measure cached environment startup (os env enter on a previously built environment) and reach < 50 ms where practical.
Native isolation (ResourceDomain + Component + capabilities) must be measurably cheaper than OCI container isolation in creation latency and memory overhead; publish the comparison.
Prototype and measure the cost of the traditional isolation path (runtime daemon, namespace setup, overlay mount, cgroups, process startup) against the native path to validate the §53 claim.
Compositor must be extremely low latency; define and measure compositor frame latency and input-to-photon latency (§54).
Measure Linux compatibility overhead (syscall latency and throughput versus upstream Linux) and track it per release (§54).
Measure Windows compatibility overhead (frame time and CPU overhead versus Proton on Linux and versus native Windows) and track it (§54).
Measure warm startup of the reference SDK application and reach the < 20 ms aspirational target (§34).
The project must never publish a performance claim that is not backed by a reproducible measurement recorded in the benchmark suite.
Performance work must prioritise changing semantics so that specific expensive operations (isolation, IPC, startup) cease to be expensive, rather than micro-optimising inherited abstractions.

Benchmark the five-step native isolation path end-to-end against a traditional Linux container start (runtime daemon, namespace setup, overlay mount, filesystem layers, cgroups, process startup) on identical hardware.
Benchmark native IPC (typed message + ownership transfer + scheduler-aware handoff) against Unix socket/pipe/D-Bus serialize-syscall-copy-deserialize paths.
Benchmark native startup (map immutable objects, reuse verified pages, launch) against traditional ELF startup (lookup, load shared libraries, resolve dependencies, run constructors).
Every architectural claim in the baseline must eventually be paired with a named benchmark; maintain a claim-to-benchmark traceability matrix in the BEN workstream.
Benchmark component creation latency (p50/p99, warm and cold).
Benchmark task creation latency (p50/p99) including creation of 500,000 tasks in one TaskGroup (cross-ref §20).
Benchmark IPC round-trip latency for small typed messages between two components on the same core.
Benchmark IPC throughput in messages per second and bytes per second for small and large messages.
Benchmark cross-core IPC latency and throughput, including cross-NUMA-node cases.
Benchmark MemoryObject transfer cost as a function of size (4 KB to multi-GB) versus memcpy of the same payload.
Benchmark application startup (launch request to first visible frame) for native demo apps.
Benchmark development environment startup for 'os env enter' (cached and uncached) against Docker Compose on Linux (cross-ref §35).
Benchmark filesystem/object access latency and throughput through capability-based storage objects versus direct Linux file I/O.
Benchmark GUI input-to-photon latency using an external photodiode/high-speed camera rig on reference hardware.
Benchmark compositor frame latency (client submit to scanout) and frame-deadline miss rate.
Benchmark Linux syscall compatibility overhead: identical syscall microbenchmarks on the fork versus the upstream kernel it was forked from.
Benchmark Windows compatibility overhead: Windows applications and games on the Windows personality versus native Windows and versus Proton on Linux.
Benchmark Linux compatibility overhead: real Linux applications on the Linux personality versus the same applications on an upstream Linux distribution.
Benchmark energy use (idle, video playback, compile, web browsing) in watt-hours on reference laptops.
Establish a Linux comparison baseline: the upstream kernel version that was forked, on identical reference hardware, for every benchmark.
Establish a Windows comparison baseline on the same reference hardware for startup, input latency, gaming and energy benchmarks.
Establish a macOS comparison baseline for benchmarks where a hardware-comparable measurement is meaningful (input-to-photon, app startup, energy).
Establish a container comparison baseline (Docker/Podman with runc and crun) for isolation creation and environment startup.
Establish language-runtime comparison baselines (Tokio, Go goroutines, Erlang/BEAM processes) for task creation, async operation cost and message passing.
Build a performance history dashboard that records every benchmark per commit on reference hardware and flags regressions beyond a per-benchmark threshold.
Decide the benchmark methodology standard: reference hardware list, warm/cold definitions, percentiles reported, iteration counts, CPU frequency pinning and mitigation settings.
Benchmark memory overhead per Component, per Task and per Channel (resident and kernel metadata).
Gaming benchmark suite (frame time distribution, input latency, load time, stutter) compared against Windows and Proton-on-Linux on the AMD desktop reference.
Do not optimise benchmark trivia while ignoring desktop UX; benchmark priorities must be tied to user-perceivable outcomes.
Measure V0 demo end-to-end latency (request submit to result received).
Measure V0 demo memory overhead per Component and per Channel.
Measure creation cost of Component, Task, TaskGroup, Channel and MemoryObject in the V0 demo against the §10 target of tens to hundreds of microseconds for Component creation.
Measure context-switch behaviour of native component handoff versus Linux thread/process switch on the same hardware.
Measure cross-core performance of the V0 demo with A and B pinned to different cores and different NUMA nodes.
Startup and input-to-photon measurements for the four demo applications recorded against the §34 target of <20 ms warm startup.
